title: Segregated dances where the crowd tore down the line
summary: He recalls dances in Rocky Mount and Durham where black and white dancers mixed.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Right. And throughout all of this time, you had separate clubs for blacks and whites?

No. Well, a lot of the places when we played, they had black and white to be there. They may not be sitting They had certain parts for them to be, together. If we were playing a white affair, then they had a place for the blacks. If you're playing blacks, they had a place for the whites.

Then, I remember one time, they had I played a dance in North Carolina in one of the warehouses. Big place, 10,000 people. Well, they just had a line between the two races. And, they started dancing. Do you know what they did? They tore that line down and everybody just started dancing. They having so much fun, were (indubidable). They took that line down. You know, right there, that was, they called it, I'm trying to think of the name. That was in Rocky Mount, North Carolina. I'll never forget it. And the funny thing, they never tried to put the line up no more. They just forgot all about it.
And that, I remember playing in Durham, North Carolina. That's where they had that big school there. The white was upstairs.
The blacks are downstairs. And, you know, it was a big stage and we played. The place was packed.
You know, they started dancing. Finally, wouldn't you know it. Everybody was down on that floor dancing together. Down there on that floor.
So, the first years I done it. As the years went along, things were different. They just forgot all about it.
